title: This Job Is Killing Me
author: Parker Houston
summary: A landmark 2021 World Health Organization and International Labour Organization study found that working more than 55 hours per week represents the leading occupational health hazard, responsible for approximately 745,000 annual deaths from stroke and heart disease. Yet research also shows that longer hours frequently produce no additional output and often harm overall productivity—knowledge workers beyond 56 hours show no measurable productivity gain compared to those working 40 hours. The causes of overwork are complex: company culture that glorifies long hours, financial pressure and debt, identity fused with career status and achievement, and lack of alternative sources of meaning. Leaders cannot solve overwork through inspiration alone. They must set explicit company policies for healthy hour expectations, model balanced work-life practices visibly, help employees build meaning outside work, and address structural pressures like mortgage and debt that force excessive work.
points: Working over 55 hours per week increases stroke risk by 35% and fatal heart disease by 17% compared to 35-40 hour weeks
Research shows that output at 70 hours differs little from output at 56 hours—the extra 14 hours are wasted time
Men disproportionately experience work-related deaths from overwork; most recorded deaths occurred between ages 60-79 for those working 55+ hours after age 45
Leaders and organizations must model healthy work hours and vacation use; what leaders catch is caught by employees
Individuals can reduce overwork by budgeting carefully, finding significance outside work, and setting a personal goal of 35-40 hours per week
quotes: Working 55 hours or more per week is a serious health hazard with documented negative health outcomes.
